You will identify a series circuit and calculate total resistance, current, voltage drops, and power. This lets you predict electrical values before building and check whether measurements make sense.

**Used in college or university:** Direct-current circuit analysis and circuit laboratories. [[1, Ch. 4]](../../references.qmd#ref-grob2016)

**Where you see it:** In a car, a lamp circuit can form one path through the battery, fuse, switch, and lamp. In a robot, a status light and current-limiting resistor form the same kind of path.

::: {.callout-note title="Read the schematic"}
Higher voltage is at the top and the 0 V or ground return is at the bottom. The battery's long line is the positive terminal. Conventional current leaves the positive rail, passes through each load, and returns to ground.
:::

## Series and parallel

A series circuit has one path, so the current is the same everywhere. A parallel circuit has branches that share the same two nodes, so each branch has the same voltage.

<figure class="ter-circuit-figure" id="fig-series-rule" data-diagram-source="../../assets/electronics/schematics/series-rule-reference.tex">
<img src="../../assets/electronics/schematics/series-rule-reference.svg" alt="Series circuit schematic showing one path through the source and resistors." loading="lazy">
<figcaption><a class="ter-figure-label" href="#fig-series-rule">Figure 1.</a> Series-circuit reference schematic. The same current passes through every component. <a class="ter-figure-anchor" href="#fig-series-rule" aria-label="Link to Figure 1">#</a></figcaption>
</figure>

Opening any component stops current everywhere.

## General rules

$$
I_k = I_T
$$ {#eq-series-current}

$$
R_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} R_k
$$ {#eq-series-resistance}

$$
V_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k
$$ {#eq-series-voltage}

$$
P_T = \sum_{k=1}^{n} P_k = V_T I_T
$$ {#eq-series-power}

$$
I_T = \frac{V_T}{R_T}
$$ {#eq-series-total-current}

$$
V_k = I_T R_k
$$ {#eq-series-component-voltage}

### How sigma notation works

$$
R_T=R_{eq}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k=R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n
$$ {#eq-series-sigma-resistance}

$$
V_T=\sum_{k=1}^{n}V_k=V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_n
$$ {#eq-series-sigma-voltage}

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $R_T$ or $R_{eq}$ | total or equivalent resistance |
| $R_k$ or $V_k$ | the value at position $k$ |
| $k$ | the index variable; it changes through $1,2,3,\ldots,n$ |
| $n$ | the fixed last index; the sum stops here |

$\Sigma$ means add each term while $k$ runs from $1$ to $n$. The final expanded term is $R_n$ or $V_n$. Keep full calculator precision until the final answer.

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} V_k \overset{?}{=} V_T
$$ {#eq-series-voltage-check}

Use Equation @eq-series-voltage-check to check the voltage drops. Also check power ratings.

## Calculate then simulate

Calculate the circuit first. Build the same series and parallel circuits in Tinkercad, measure current and voltage, then compare the calculated and simulated values.

## Worked solutions {#worked-solutions}

Questions 2 and 4 are provided as student models. Complete the other questions independently using the same GUESS structure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Question 2: Complete series analysis" #question-2-complete-series-analysis}
**Given:** $V_T=15.0\,\mathrm{V}$, $R_1=1.0\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, $R_2=2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, $R_3=3.3\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$.

$$
R_T=R_1+R_2+R_3=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
$$ {#eq-series-worked-q2-resistance}

$$
I_T=\frac{V_T}{R_T}=\frac{15.0\,\mathrm{V}}{6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}
$$ {#eq-series-worked-q2-current}

Using $V_k=I_TR_k$ gives $V_1=2.307692\ldots\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_2=5.076923\ldots\,\mathrm{V}$, and $V_3=7.615385\ldots\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Final answers:** $R_T=6.5\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, $I_T=2.3\,\mathrm{mA}$, $V_1=2.3\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_2=5.1\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_3=7.6\,\mathrm{V}$, and $P_T=35\,\mathrm{mW}$.

**Check:** Use the unrounded values: $V_1+V_2+V_3=15.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Question 4: Choose a dropping resistor" #question-4-choose-a-dropping-resistor}
**Given:** a $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$, $80\,\mathrm{mA}$ lamp on a $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ source.

$$
V_R=V_T-V_L=9.0\,\mathrm{V}-6.0\,\mathrm{V}=3.0\,\mathrm{V}
$$ {#eq-series-worked-q4-voltage}

$$
R=\frac{V_R}{I}=\frac{3.0\,\mathrm{V}}{80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}}=37.5\,\Omega
$$ {#eq-series-worked-q4-resistance}

$$
P_R=V_RI=(3.0\,\mathrm{V})(80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A})=0.240\,\mathrm{W}
$$ {#eq-series-worked-q4-power}

**Final answer:** the calculated value is $37.5\,\Omega$. Choose the next common 5% value, $39\,\Omega$, rated for at least $0.5\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Key note:** A $0.25\,\mathrm{W}$ resistor is too close to the calculated $0.240\,\mathrm{W}$ load.
:::
